lesson.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main and resolve conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main and resolve conflicts

steps.title: Recreate the example repository
steps.instructions: In the empty folder run `git init -b main`, commit a `login.txt` with one line, then `git checkout -b feature/login` and make three commits (1st and 3rd change that line, 2nd only adds `notes.txt`). Switch to main, make two commits changing the same line of `login.txt` differently, then `git checkout feature/login`.

targets.caption: Finish on the feature branch, ready to rebase

explanations.topic: Rebase sets your feature commits aside and reapplies them one by one, so each can conflict
Feature branch's three commits originate from a commit on main that has since gained two commits
Making main's latest commit the new base of the feature branch
Repo is set up so two feature commits conflict and the notes.txt commit does not

hints: Create the feature branch from main's first commit, before main gets its extra commits.
Feature commits 1 and 3 must edit the same line of login.txt; commit 2 only adds notes.txt.
On main, make two commits that edit that same line of login.txt in a different way.
Check with `git log --oneline --graph --all` that both branches diverge from the first commit, then `git checkout feature/login`.
common_mistakes: Adding main's two commits before creating feature/login, so there is nothing to rebase.
Editing a different line, so the rebase produces no conflicts.
Forgetting `git add` before committing, leaving changes uncommitted.
Staying on main at the end instead of switching back to feature/login.
Using an older git without `-b` support for `git init`; use `git init` then `git checkout -b main`.
steps.code:
git init -b main
echo "login v1" > login.txt
git add login.txt && git commit -m "Add login"
git checkout -b feature/login
# commit 1: change the line in login.txt
# commit 2: add notes.txt only
# commit 3: change the same line in login.txt again
git checkout main
# two commits each changing the same line of login.txt differently
git checkout feature/login

steps.title: Start the rebase onto main
steps.instructions: On feature/login run `git rebase main` and watch it stop on the first conflict in login.txt. Run `git status` to confirm the rebase is in progress and how many commits remain.

targets.caption: Git pauses the rebase at the first conflicting commit
git status confirms the rebase is paused, not finished
How many commits are still left to replay

explanations.topic: A conflict pauses the rebase, it doesn't abort it
git status shows which commit failed and how many remain
Resolving rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts: Git puts conflict markers in the conflicted files

hints: Make sure you're on your feature branch first (git branch shows the current one), then rebase onto main.
Run `git rebase main` from the feature branch, then `git status`.
Look at the 'Last command done' and 'Next commands to do' sections of git status to find the failing commit and the remaining count.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while on main instead of the feature branch, which gives 'Current branch main is up to date'.
Thinking the rebase failed and running `git rebase --abort` instead of resolving the conflict.
Using `git merge main` instead of rebase, so no rebase is in progress.
Main lacking the conflicting commits from step 1, so the rebase succeeds with no conflict.

steps.title: Resolve the first conflict
steps.instructions: Open login.txt, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers and keep the line that should stay. Stage it with `git add login.txt` and run `git status`.

targets.caption: Delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, keeping the code that should stay
Stage the resolved file, then run git status to confirm

explanations.topic: Remove the markers, pick the code that should stay, then git add every conflicted file
Unlike a merge, you don't commit; you run git rebase --continue next
During a rebase you run git rebase --continue instead of committing

hints: Run git status to see which files are listed under 'both modified' or 'Unmerged paths'.
Open login.txt in your editor. The lines between <<<<<<< and ======= are one side and the lines between ======= and >>>>>>> are the other. Decide which code should stay.
Delete all three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and any unwanted code, then save the file.
Run git add login.txt, then git status. It should say all conflicts are fixed and suggest git rebase --continue.
common_mistakes: Leaving one of the marker lines (often =======) in the file.
Forgetting to save the file before running git add.
Running git commit instead of staging and moving on to git rebase --continue.
Running git rebase --abort by accident, which throws away the rebase in progress.
Staging only some of the conflicted files when there are several.

steps.title: Continue the rebase in vim
steps.instructions: Run `git rebase --continue`; when vim opens press Escape, type `:wq` and Enter. Git applies the notes.txt commit automatically and pauses again on the third commit.

targets.caption: Continue the rebase instead of committing
Save and quit vim to keep the commit message
Git pauses again on the third commit

explanations.topic: Git opens vim to edit the commit message; Escape then :wq saves and quits
Git auto-applies the non-conflicting second commit and stops on the third
Git pauses again because the third and last commit conflicts

hints: After staging the resolved file, run git rebase --continue rather than git commit.
When vim opens, you don't need to change the message: press Escape first so you're in normal mode.
Then type :wq and press Enter to save and close. Git will apply the next commits on its own.
Seeing a new CONFLICT afterwards is expected here: the third commit conflicts again, and that is fixed in the next step.
common_mistakes: Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue during the rebase.
Forgetting to git add the resolved file first, so git says 'you must edit all merge conflicts'.
Typing :wq while still in insert mode (without pressing Escape), which inserts the text into the message.
Getting stuck in vim and closing the terminal, leaving the rebase half-finished.
Thinking the new CONFLICT means something went wrong, then running git rebase --abort.

steps.title: Fix last conflict and finish
steps.instructions: Resolve the markers in login.txt again, `git add login.txt` and run `git rebase --continue`, saving with `:wq`. Run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` to verify the feature commits sit on top of main.

precision_checks.label: No rebase directory remains
precision_checks.command: test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-merge)" && test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-apply)"

targets.caption: Git finishes replaying the last feature commit
git status confirms you're out of the rebasing state

explanations.topic: With no commits left, rebase --continue concludes the rebase
Using git status to confirm you're no longer rebasing

hints: Fix this conflict exactly as you did the first one: open the file and look for the conflict markers.
Remove every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line, keeping the content you want, then save the file.
Stage it with git add <file>, run git rebase --continue, and in vim type :wq to accept the message.
Run git status: it should say 'On branch ...' with no mention of a rebase in progress; git log --oneline --graph should show feature commits on top of main.
common_mistakes: Leaving a stray conflict marker (e.g. =======) in the file before git add.
Running git rebase --continue without first git add-ing the resolved file.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue, leaving the rebase unfinished.
Getting stuck in vim: press Esc before typing :wq.
Running git rebase --abort by mistake, which throws away the whole rebase.
steps.run_command: git add <conflicted-file> && git rebase --continue  # save the commit message in vim with :wq, then: git status
